steps.title: Import Vue and composition API functions
steps.instruction: Import Vue, ref, and computed from 'vue'
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the necessary Vue functionality. You'll need these for creating reactive state and computed properties.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing multiple items from a module
import { createApp, reactive } from 'vue'
steps.seedCode: // Import Vue, ref, and computed from 'vue'
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement will be added to the file, making Vue and its composition API functions available for use.
successCriteria: Vue, ref, and computed are imported from 'vue'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported Vue, ref, and computed. These are essential for working with Vue's composition API.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing all three items: Vue, ref, and computed from 'vue'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import Vue, ref, and computed from the 'vue' module using the import statement.

steps.title: Create the main Vue component
steps.instruction: Create a Vue component named 'StableReferencesDemo' with a setup function that returns an empty object.
steps.hint: Define a component using Vue's composition API. The setup function should return an object (even if empty for now).
steps.expectedOutcome: A Vue component named StableReferencesDemo is created with a setup function that returns an empty object.
successCriteria: The component is named StableReferencesDemo, has a setup function, and returns an empty object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main Vue component structure. The setup function will hold our reactive state and logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have: 1) Component named StableReferencesDemo, 2) A setup() function, 3) Returns an empty object {}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component structure isn't quite right. Check that you have a component named StableReferencesDemo with a setup function returning an empty object.

steps.title: Initialize reactive state with ref
steps.instruction: Inside the setup function, declare a reactive state variable called 'count' using ref and initialize it to 0.
steps.hint: Use the ref function imported earlier to create a reactive reference with an initial value of 0.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating reactive state
const message = ref('Hello');
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a reactive count state variable initialized to 0, ready to be used in the UI and handlers.
successCriteria: A count variable is declared using ref with an initial value of 0 inside the setup function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created reactive state using ref. This count variable will maintain reactivity throughout the component's lifecycle.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using ref to create the reactive state and initializing it to 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: The count state wasn't properly initialized. Remember to use ref(0) to create a reactive reference with initial value 0.

steps.title: Create a regular function without useCallback
steps.instruction: Inside the setup function, create a regular function named increment that increases the count state by 1.
steps.hint: Define a function that updates the count value using count.value += 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: A regular increment function is defined inside the setup function that modifies the count state.
successCriteria: The increment function is defined without useCallback and updates count.value by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a regular function that updates the count. This function will be recreated on every render.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but make sure it updates count.value by 1 and is placed inside the setup function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The increment function should be defined inside setup and update count.value by 1. Try again.

steps.title: Add a button that uses the regular function
steps.instruction: In the setup function's return object, add a button element with the text 'Increment (Regular)' and wire its click event to call the regular increment function.
steps.hint: Use @click to bind the click event to your increment function. The button should be inside the return object.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button that calls a function
<button @click="handleClick">Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Increment (Regular)' appears in the UI, which when clicked will call the regular increment function.
successCriteria: The return object contains a button element with @click bound to incrementRegular and the text 'Increment (Regular)'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully connected the regular function to a button click event.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the button has both the correct text and the @click binding to incrementRegular.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly connected to the increment function. Check the button's text and click event binding.

steps.title: Add a second button that also uses the regular function
steps.instruction: In the return object of your setup function, add a second button that also calls the incrementRegular function when clicked.
steps.hint: Add another button element with an @click handler that calls incrementRegular.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding another button with the same handler
<button @click="incrementRegular">Increment Again</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have two buttons that both increment the count using the same regular function.
successCriteria: A second button is added to the return object with an @click handler that calls incrementRegular.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a second button that uses the same incrementRegular function.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a second button, but make sure it calls incrementRegular when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The second button is missing or doesn't call incrementRegular correctly.

steps.title: Import computed for derived state
steps.instruction: Add computed to the existing import statement from 'vue'.
steps.hint: Update the import line to include computed alongside ref.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing multiple Vue APIs
import { ref, computed } from 'vue';
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement now includes computed, making it available for creating derived reactive state.
successCriteria: computed is imported from 'vue' in the same statement as ref.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've imported computed, which will allow you to create derived reactive state in the next steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure computed is included in the import statement from 'vue'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to add computed to the existing import statement from 'vue'.

steps.title: Create a computed property
steps.instruction: Inside the setup function, create a computed property named 'countParity' that returns a string indicating whether count is 'even' or 'odd'.
steps.hint: Use the computed function imported from Vue to create a derived reactive value. The computed function takes a getter function that returns the derived value based on count.value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: computed property for derived state
const doubleCount = computed(() => count.value * 2);
steps.expectedOutcome: A computed property 'countParity' is created that returns 'even' when count is even and 'odd' when count is odd.
successCriteria: The computed property 'countParity' is defined inside setup and returns a string based on count.value % 2.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a computed property that derives state from count.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure countParity returns 'even' or 'odd' based on count.value % 2.
steps.feedbackWrong: The computed property isn't correctly defined. Use computed(() => count.value % 2 === 0 ? 'even' : 'odd').

steps.title: Display the computed property in the template
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your setup function, add a paragraph element that displays the computed property value.
steps.hint: You can access the computed property value directly in the template. Use double curly braces to display it.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying a computed value

Computed value: {{ computedValue }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The computed property value will be displayed in the UI, automatically updating when the count changes.
successCriteria: A paragraph element exists in the return statement
The paragraph displays the computed property value using template syntax
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully displayed the computed property value in the template. This shows how computed properties automatically update in the UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added a paragraph element in the return statement that displays the computed property value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The computed property value isn't being displayed in the template. Add a paragraph element that shows the computed value.

steps.title: Add a reset button with a new function
steps.instruction: Inside the setup function, create a new function named resetCount that sets the count value back to 0.
steps.hint: Define a function that updates count.value to 0.
steps.expectedOutcome: A resetCount function is defined that can reset the count state to 0.
successCriteria: The resetCount function is defined and sets count.value to 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a reset function. This demonstrates how new functions can be added to manage state changes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but make sure it sets count.value to 0 and is named resetCount.
steps.feedbackWrong: The resetCount function isn't defined correctly. Create a function that sets count.value to 0.
